subject: Economics
topic: Market Structures — Perfect Competition to Monopoly
description: Covers market structures: perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly, monopsony — with India-specific regulatory context.

questions.stem: Which market structure has a single seller who controls the entire supply of a product with no close substitutes?

options.option_text: Monopoly — sole seller, high barriers to entry, price-maker
Oligopoly — few large sellers dominate the market
Monopolistic competition — many sellers with differentiated products
Perfect competition — many sellers of identical products

questions.explanation: MONOPOLY has one seller controlling the entire supply. Key features: No close substitutes; High barriers to entry (legal, natural, or technological); Firm is a PRICE-MAKER not price-taker; Can earn supernormal profits long-run. Types: (1) NATURAL MONOPOLY — high fixed costs make one firm most efficient (e.g., railways, water supply). (2) LEGAL MONOPOLY — government grants exclusive rights (e.g., patents, licences). (3) PURE MONOPOLY — no substitutes at all. INDIA EXAMPLES: Indian Railways (near-natural monopoly in rail transport); BSNL had near-monopoly before liberalisation. REGULATION: Competition Commission of India (CCI) under Competition Act 2002 prevents abuse of dominant position. MEMORY AID: Mono = One. PYQ: SSC CGL, UPSC GS-3, IBPS PO every cycle.

questions.stem: Perfect competition is characterised by which combination of features?

options.option_text: Many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry/exit, perfect information — each firm is a price-taker
Few sellers, differentiated products, significant entry barriers, price leadership by dominant firm
Single buyer facing many sellers, monopsony power, wage depression in labour markets
Two sellers competing on price until marginal cost pricing equilibrium is reached

questions.explanation: PERFECT COMPETITION — 4 defining conditions: (1) MANY BUYERS AND SELLERS — no single actor influences price. (2) HOMOGENEOUS PRODUCT — goods are identical (e.g., wheat, rice). (3) FREE ENTRY AND EXIT — no barriers; long-run only normal profits. (4) PERFECT INFORMATION — all buyers/sellers know all prices. RESULT: Each firm is a PRICE-TAKER — must accept the market price. LONG-RUN EQUILIBRIUM: P = MC = AC (no supernormal profit). REAL-WORLD APPROXIMATION: Agricultural commodity markets (wheat, onion) come closest. COMMON TRAP: Perfect competition is a theoretical ideal — no real market perfectly satisfies all four conditions. MEMORY AID: Perfect = 4 perfect conditions. PYQ: SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims GS-3, CA Foundation.

questions.stem: Oligopoly is best described as a market structure where:

options.option_text: A few large firms dominate, each interdependent — one firm's pricing decision affects and triggers reactions from rivals
Hundreds of small firms sell slightly differentiated products with easy entry and exit
A single buyer has market power over many small suppliers, suppressing input prices
Two equal-sized firms collude to set a monopoly price and split profits equally

questions.explanation: OLIGOPOLY — Key Features: (1) FEW LARGE SELLERS — each has significant market share. (2) INTERDEPENDENCE — each firm must consider rivals' reactions before changing price/output. (3) HIGH ENTRY BARRIERS — capital, technology, or brand loyalty. (4) PRODUCTS — may be homogeneous (steel, cement) or differentiated (cars, smartphones). KEY MODELS: PRICE LEADERSHIP — dominant firm sets price, others follow. KINKED DEMAND CURVE (Sweezy) — explains price rigidity in oligopolies. CARTEL — explicit collusion to behave like a monopoly (e.g., OPEC). INDIA EXAMPLES: Telecom (Jio, Airtel, Vi), cement industry, aviation sector. COMPETITION ACT 2002: Anti-cartel provisions enforced by CCI. PYQ: UPSC GS-3, IBPS PO, SSC CGL Tier 2.

questions.stem: Monopolistic competition differs from pure monopoly primarily because in monopolistic competition:

options.option_text: There are many sellers with slightly differentiated products and relatively easy entry, preventing long-run supernormal profits
A single seller controls the entire market with absolute barriers to entry preventing competition
Products are perfectly identical and price is determined entirely by market forces of supply and demand
Firms explicitly collude to set uniform prices and divide the market geographically among themselves

questions.explanation: MONOPOLISTIC COMPETITION — combines features of both perfect competition AND monopoly. FEATURES: (1) MANY SELLERS — like perfect competition. (2) DIFFERENTIATED PRODUCTS — each firm has a mini-monopoly over its own brand (like monopoly). (3) RELATIVELY EASY ENTRY/EXIT — supernormal profits attract new entrants long-run. LONG-RUN RESULT: Supernormal profits disappear as entry increases; only normal profit remains, but P > MC (unlike perfect competition where P = MC). PRODUCT DIFFERENTIATION TOOLS: Quality, branding, packaging, location, after-sales service. INDIA EXAMPLES: Restaurants, garment retail, STD/ISD booths, coaching institutes. CHAMBERLIN's MODEL: E.H. Chamberlin developed the monopolistic competition model in 1933. MEMORY AID: Monopolistic competition = Many sellers + My brand is unique. PYQ: UPSC GS-3, SSC CGL.

questions.stem: The concept of 'deadweight loss' in monopoly refers to:

options.option_text: The net welfare loss to society because monopoly restricts output below and prices above the competitive equilibrium, eliminating mutually beneficial transactions
The loss in monopoly profits caused by government price controls set below the profit-maximising level
Fixed costs that cannot be recovered when a monopoly firm exits the market after a price war
Tax revenue lost to the government because monopolies shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions

questions.explanation: DEADWEIGHT LOSS IN MONOPOLY: Under perfect competition: P = MC, output = Q*. Under monopoly: P > MC, output = Qm < Q*. MECHANISM: (1) Monopoly restricts output to raise price above MC. (2) SOME MUTUALLY BENEFICIAL TRANSACTIONS that would have occurred at competitive price are eliminated. (3) Consumer surplus and producer surplus that would have existed are DESTROYED — not transferred, but lost to society permanently. GRAPHICALLY: The deadweight loss triangle lies between the competitive and monopoly output levels. POLICY IMPLICATIONS: (1) Government regulates natural monopolies (e.g., electricity, water) via price caps. (2) Competition Commission prevents monopolistic abuse. (3) Antitrust actions break up or regulate dominant firms. INDIA: CCI can impose penalties up to 10% of average 3-year turnover for abuse of dominant position. PYQ: UPSC GS-3, RBI Grade-B, CA Foundation.

questions.stem: Monopsony describes a market where there is a single buyer. Which real-world scenario in India best exemplifies monopsony power?

options.option_text: A single state electricity board being the only buyer of power from multiple small renewable energy producers in its grid territory
A single large cement company controlling all cement production in a region and setting retail prices
A government-run food corporation purchasing all agricultural output at minimum support prices from farmers across India
A dominant e-commerce platform charging sellers a fixed commission regardless of product category or sales volume

questions.explanation: MONOPSONY — SINGLE BUYER market power. Key Feature: Buyer sets the price (wage/input price) below competitive level; suppliers/workers have no alternative buyer. WELFARE EFFECT: Input suppliers receive LESS than their marginal revenue product — analogous to monopoly exploiting consumers. INDIA EXAMPLES: (1) STATE ELECTRICITY BOARDS (SEBs/DISCOMs) — often the sole licensed buyer of power in their territory; renewable energy producers must sell to them. (2) Tobacco companies as sole buyers from tobacco farmers in Andhra Pradesh/Karnataka. (3) Tea estate owners in remote hill regions as sole employers of tribal labour (wage monopsony). LABOUR MARKET MONOPSONY: When a single employer dominates local labour markets — nurses at the only hospital in a small town. POLICY: Electricity Act 2003 introduced open access to reduce SEB monopsony. PYQ: UPSC GS-3, RBI Grade-B, IBPS PO Mains.

questions.stem: Natural monopoly arises when a firm's long-run average cost curve declines continuously over the relevant range of market demand. What is the PRIMARY policy challenge this creates for regulators?

options.option_text: Setting price equal to marginal cost (efficient pricing) causes losses since MC < AC, requiring either government subsidies or above-marginal-cost regulated prices
Natural monopolies always earn supernormal profits that must be taxed away fully to prevent wealth concentration
Continuous entry of competitors erodes the natural monopoly's cost advantage, creating market instability
Natural monopolies produce public goods that cannot be priced at all, requiring direct government provision only

questions.explanation: NATURAL MONOPOLY REGULATION DILEMMA: A natural monopoly has continuously declining LRAC — average cost falls as output rises. One large firm can serve the entire market cheaper than multiple small firms. REGULATORY OPTIONS AND TRADE-OFFS: (1) MARGINAL COST PRICING (P = MC): Economically EFFICIENT but causes a LOSS because MC < AC. Government must subsidise the loss — creating taxpayer burden. (2) AVERAGE COST PRICING (P = AC): Firm breaks even (normal profit), no subsidy needed, but P > MC — slight inefficiency. (3) TWO-PART TARIFF: Fixed connection fee + per-unit price at MC — can recover costs while maintaining efficiency. (4) RATE-OF-RETURN REGULATION: Allows a fair rate of return on capital — used for Indian power tariffs by CERC/SERCs. INDIA EXAMPLES: Indian Railways, ONGC pipelines, PowerGrid transmission. PYQ: UPSC GS-3, RBI Grade-B, NABARD Grade-A.

questions.stem: In perfect competition, a firm is a price taker. What is the correct relationship between Average Revenue (AR), Marginal Revenue (MR), and market price (P) at every level of output for such a firm?

options.option_text: AR exceeds MR because the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve
AR, MR, and P are all equal; the firm's demand curve is perfectly flat
MR is always below AR, as the firm must cut price to sell additional units
AR equals market price, but MR declines steadily as output expands

questions.explanation: B is correct because a perfectly competitive firm sells every unit at the same market price P, so TR = P × Q, AR = TR/Q = P, and MR = ΔTR/ΔQ = P. Hence AR = MR = P at all output levels and the firm's demand curve is a horizontal line at P. Options A and C describe a monopolist or monopolistic competitor whose downward-sloping demand curve forces MR below AR. Option D is similarly wrong — declining MR is a feature of imperfect competition, not perfect competition.

questions.stem: In the long-run equilibrium of monopolistic competition, firms earn only normal profits. Which statement correctly describes the price–cost relationship at this equilibrium?

options.option_text: Firms earn supernormal profits as product differentiation sustains entry barriers
Price equals minimum long-run average cost, exactly mirroring perfect competition
Firms earn only normal profit while price remains above the minimum average cost
Output expands to the socially optimal level, and all excess capacity is eliminated

questions.explanation: C is correct. Free entry erodes supernormal profits until AR = LAC (normal profit). However, since each firm's demand curve slopes downward, the tangency with the LAC curve occurs on its falling portion — not at its minimum. Thus P > minimum LAC and firms carry excess capacity. Option B is the perfect competition outcome where a flat demand curve forces tangency at minimum LAC. Option A describes only the short-run position before entry occurs. Option D is wrong because excess capacity is a defining, not eliminated, feature of this long-run equilibrium.

questions.stem: The kinked demand curve model (Paul Sweezy, 1939) explains price stickiness in oligopoly. What is the direct implication of this 'kink' for the firm's Marginal Revenue (MR) curve?

options.option_text: MR becomes zero at the kink, marking the revenue-maximising output for the firm
MR has a vertical discontinuity at the kink, so moderate MC shifts leave price unchanged
MR equals price at the kink, since rivals symmetrically match every price adjustment
MR turns upward at the kink, reflecting rivals' increased responsiveness to price cuts

questions.explanation: B is correct. The kink arises because rivals follow price cuts (making demand inelastic below the kink) but ignore price hikes (making demand elastic above the kink). This discontinuity in slope creates a vertical gap in the MR curve directly below the kink. As long as the firm's MC curve passes through this gap, the profit-maximising output and price remain constant — explaining price rigidity without formal collusion. Option A confuses MR = 0 with the revenue-maximising point, an unrelated concept. Option C incorrectly assumes rivals respond symmetrically, which is the opposite of Sweezy's behavioural assumption.

questions.stem: A monopolist can practice third-degree price discrimination by charging different prices in two separate markets. Beyond having market power and differing demand elasticities, which condition is strictly necessary to prevent arbitrage from collapsing the price differential?

options.option_text: The monopolist must hold a government patent giving exclusive production rights
Each market must be sealed so consumers cannot resell the good between segments
Every consumer segment must individually face a perfectly inelastic demand curve
Total market demand must be highly price-elastic to justify splitting the markets

questions.explanation: B is correct. If buyers in the low-price segment could resell to buyers in the high-price segment, the price gap would be arbitraged away, making discrimination unsustainable. Market separation — geographic, institutional, or by product form — prevents this. Option A confers market power but does not address arbitrage. Option C is wrong: perfectly inelastic demand everywhere would yield the same optimal price in both segments, eliminating any reason to discriminate. Option D is the opposite of what is required; discrimination is most valuable when elasticities differ markedly across segments.

questions.stem: The 'excess capacity theorem' identifies a market structure in which long-run equilibrium output falls below the technically efficient scale. To which structure does this theorem specifically apply, and what causes it?

options.option_text: Perfect competition, where free entry drives price to the minimum of long-run AC
Pure monopoly, where the firm permanently restricts output to earn supernormal profits
Monopolistic competition, where downward-sloping demand causes tangency above minimum AC
Oligopoly under Cournot competition, where strategic rivalry generates deadweight loss

questions.explanation: C is correct. In long-run monopolistic competition, free entry drives profits to zero (AR = LAC), but the downward-sloping demand curve means this tangency occurs on the falling segment of LAC, not at its minimum. The gap between actual output and minimum-AC output is the 'excess capacity.' Option A is wrong because in perfect competition, the horizontal demand curve forces tangency exactly at minimum LAC — no excess capacity exists. Option B is wrong because monopoly involves persistent supernormal profit, not a zero-profit free-entry equilibrium; the theorem's mechanism requires free entry.

questions.stem: A profit-maximising monopolist faces a constant marginal cost of ₹100 and the absolute price elasticity of demand at the chosen output is |η| = 2. Using the Lerner Index, what is the profit-maximising price?

options.option_text: ₹150, from misapplying the mark-up as (P − MC)/MC = 1/|η|, giving P = 150
₹200, from Lerner Index (P − MC)/P = 1/|η|, so P = MC × |η|/(|η| − 1)
₹133, from erroneously applying the Cournot duopoly mark-up rule with n = 2
₹300, from inverting the formula as P = MC × (|η| + 1)/(|η| − 1) = 300

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Lerner Index states (P − MC)/P = 1/|η|. Rearranging: P(1 − 1/|η|) = MC → P = MC × |η|/(|η| − 1) = 100 × 2/(2 − 1) = ₹200. Verification: (200 − 100)/200 = 0.5 = 1/2 ✓. Option A confuses the denominator, using (P − MC)/MC = 0.5, giving P − 100 = 50 → ₹150. Option C wrongly applies the Cournot symmetric n-firm formula (P − MC)/P = 1/(n|η|) = 1/4, yielding P ≈ ₹133. Option D uses an erroneously inverted numerator, (|η| + 1)/(|η| − 1) = 3, giving ₹300.

questions.stem: In the dominant firm model of price leadership, the dominant firm sets the market price while competitive fringe firms act as price takers at that price. Which curve does the dominant firm construct to determine its profit-maximising output and price?

options.option_text: Full market demand curve, applying monopoly optimisation directly like a pure monopolist
Residual demand curve obtained by subtracting fringe supply from total market demand
Kinked demand curve incorporating fringe firms' asymmetric price-response behaviour
Pooled supply curve combining dominant and fringe output at each possible market price

questions.explanation: B is correct. The dominant firm first derives how much the competitive fringe will supply at each price (the fringe supply schedule). It subtracts this from total market demand to obtain its residual demand curve — the quantity it alone can sell at each price. It then computes the MR from this residual demand, sets MR = MC, and announces the resulting price, which the fringe accepts. Option A is wrong because using full market demand ignores fringe supply, causing the dominant firm to over-estimate its captive volume. Option C confuses this model with the Sweezy kinked-demand framework, which applies to symmetric oligopolists lacking a dominant price leader.
